pinterest.title: Lebanese Wedding Traditions: The Customs and What They Mean
pinterest.description: A guide to Lebanese wedding traditions in the order families usually keep them: the formal asking (tulbeh), the engagement (khutbeh), the henna night, a church crowning or katb al-kitab, the zaffeh entrance, the dabke, zaghareet, the sword at the cake and sugared almonds. Written for Lebanese-Australian and mixed-heritage couples planning a wedding in Italy, Cyprus, the UAE or Australia.

pinterest.title: The Lebanese Henna Night (Laylat al-Henna): A Pre-Wedding Evening
pinterest.description: In Lebanese families who keep it, the henna night is often told as an intimate evening: the women of both families, a tray of henna, songs and the bride at the centre. Some families call it by other names, and some skip it. Planning a destination wedding? Hold it once close family has landed and slept, usually two nights before the wedding. Read the full guide to Lebanese wedding traditions.

pinterest.title: Sugared Almonds at Lebanese Weddings: Mlabbas and Wedding Sweets
pinterest.description: Families often serve mlabbas (sugar-coated almonds) at the engagement and the wedding, in small favour bags or bowls on every table, alongside trays of Lebanese sweets late in the night. Their meaning is often told simply: sweetness for the marriage, and something for every guest to take home. More Lebanese wedding traditions and their meaning in our guide.

slides: A Lebanese wedding rarely starts on the wedding day. Here are the customs families keep, and what they mean.

Before the wedding: the tulbeh, the formal asking, is a private family visit, and Arabic coffee is often part of it. Then the khutbeh, the engagement, is often a family dinner where rings are exchanged.
The henna night (laylat al-henna): in families who keep it, it is often told as an intimate evening. The women of both families, a tray of henna, songs, and the bride at the centre.
The marriage itself: many Christian couples marry in Eastern churches, where the heart of the service is the crowning. For many Muslim families, it is the katb al-kitab, the signing of the contract.
The zaffeh: the procession that brings the couple in. It is often told as drummers, dancers and singers leading the way, with guests clapping them in.
The dabke: dancers move in a line holding handkerchiefs high, and the first in the row signals each step. At weddings, many families invite everyone into the line.
Zaghareet, a sword at the cake and sugared almonds (mlabbas) for every table: sweetness for the marriage, and something for each guest to take home.
Bringing these customs to Italy, Cyprus, the UAE or Australia? Message us and a Wedded Advisor will talk through the venue questions with you.
instagram_carousel.caption:
There is no single Lebanese wedding. Lebanese families are Christian, Muslim and Druze, and customs vary between families, regions and households. Most draw on the same set of traditions, in roughly this order: the formal asking (tulbeh), the engagement (khutbeh), the henna night (laylat al-henna), a church crowning or a katb al-kitab, the zaffeh entrance, the dabke, zaghareet, cutting the cake with a sword, and sugared almonds and sweets.

The practical point for planning: ask both families early which steps they want, rather than working from a list.

Carrying these customs to a wedding abroad? Each one asks something of the venue. A zaffeh needs a route, not just a doorway. A dabke line needs a long run of floor rather than a small square. Drums are loud, so ask about music finish times and rules on live percussion outdoors.
